introduction-from-cloud-first-to-cloud-s.core: 'Cloud first' assumed the cloud is always best. 'Cloud smart' recognises that stable, large, predictable workloads can be cheaper on owned or colocated hardware, while elastic or innovative work belongs in the cloud. Choose per workload.

first_principles.problem: Companies with steady, massive workloads pay a premium for elasticity they never use.
truths: Cloud pricing includes a premium for flexibility.
derivation: Compare **TCO**: cloud vs colocation vs hybrid.

analogy.title: Living in a hotel vs. buying a house
analogy.story: Hotels are great for short or uncertain stays; for a decade in one city, buying wins.
analogy.breaks: Repatriation adds operational burden. Not every team can run hardware well.

example.title: A workload split

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each workload on its most economical platform.

example.outcome: placement driven by economics, not dogma.

check.q: What kind of workload is the best candidate for repatriation?
check.a: Large, steady, predictable workloads that don't benefit from cloud elasticity.

the-economics-rent-vs-buy.core: Cloud is renting: no upfront capital, instant scale and managed operations, at a premium per unit. Owning has high upfront cost and operational responsibility, but over 3–5 years can cost far less for steady, high utilisation.

first_principles.problem: Teams compare a cloud monthly bill with server purchase prices and ignore power, space, staff and refresh cycles.
truths: Utilisation determines the effective cost of owned hardware.
People and facilities are real costs.
derivation: **Cloud TCO**: compute + storage + egress + managed services.
**Owned TCO**: hardware + colo space/power + network + staff + refresh.

analogy.title: A hotel stay vs. a mortgage
analogy.story: Short term, the hotel's room service and flexibility win; over five years, the mortgage is far cheaper per night.
analogy.breaks: Low utilisation of owned hardware destroys its advantage.

example.title: A 5-year TCO comparison

steps.label: Caveat
steps.detail: That assumes the team can operate it reliably.

example.outcome: rent-vs-buy decisions based on full TCO.

check.q: Which factor most determines whether owning hardware beats cloud?
check.a: Sustained high utilisation over a multi-year horizon, plus the ability to operate it efficiently.

case-study-the-37signals-exit.core: 37signals (Basecamp, HEY) moved steady workloads from AWS to owned servers in colocation, projecting about $7M in savings over five years. It shows repatriation works for predictable SaaS with a capable ops team, while they still use the cloud selectively.

first_principles.problem: The debate needs concrete evidence rather than ideology.
truths: Their workloads were stable and well understood.
Hardware was bought at a fraction of the cloud's annual cost.
derivation: **Kept S3** initially, then planned storage exit.

analogy.title: A family that stopped renting after years in the same town
analogy.story: Once you know you're staying, buying the house pays off.
analogy.breaks: Their success depended on predictable growth and a strong ops team, which doesn't generalise everywhere.

example.title: Their published numbers (approx.)

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: The economics favour owning for steady, large, simple workloads.

example.outcome: a concrete reference point for repatriation decisions.

check.q: What preconditions made 37signals' cloud exit successful?
check.a: Stable, predictable workloads and an experienced in-house operations team.

colocation-the-middle-ground.core: Colocation rents space, power, cooling and connectivity in a professional data centre, while you own and run the servers. It avoids building facilities while still getting hardware economics.

first_principles.problem: 'Going on-prem' sounds like building a data centre with generators, which is unrealistic for most companies.
truths: Colo providers offer cross-connects to clouds and carriers.
derivation: Rent **racks or cages** with power and cooling.
**Cross-connect** to clouds for a hybrid setup.

analogy.title: Renting a commercial kitchen space
analogy.story: You bring your own equipment and chefs, but the building, gas and safety systems are provided.
analogy.breaks: You still own hardware lifecycle, spares and capacity planning.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Hardware economics without building a data centre.

check.q: What does a colocation provider supply?
check.a: Physical space, power, cooling, security and network connectivity for your own servers.

the-hidden-costs-of-exit-egress-fees-and.core: Leaving the cloud means moving data out, and egress fees on petabytes are substantial. Data gravity (services, analytics and integrations clustered around large datasets) makes moving even harder.

first_principles.problem: A company planning to exit discovers that moving 5 PB out costs hundreds of thousands in egress, plus months of transfer time.
truths: Ingress is free; egress is charged.
Large data takes time to move.
derivation: **Quantify egress** (PB × $/GB, minus negotiated or waived exit fees).
**Negotiate exit waivers** (some providers now offer them).

analogy.title: Moving house with a lifetime of belongings
analogy.story: The more you've accumulated, the costlier and slower the move, and the more things are tied to the old address.
analogy.breaks: Major providers announced egress waivers for full exits in 2024, so check current terms.

example.title: Estimating a data exit

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No surprises in the exit budget.

example.outcome: exit plans that account for data gravity.

check.a: The tendency of large datasets to attract dependent services and integrations, making them hard and costly to move.

exit-strategy-keeping-your-options-open.core: Design for portability from day one: containers and Kubernetes, open-source data stores, IaC, abstraction at key boundaries, and data in open formats, so leaving (or negotiating) stays possible without rewriting everything.

first_principles.problem: Deep use of proprietary services makes exit prohibitively expensive, which also removes negotiation leverage.
truths: Full portability has its own cost.
derivation: Prefer **open data stores and formats** (Postgres, Parquet).
Keep a **documented exit plan** and test pieces of it.

analogy.title: Keeping your passport valid
analogy.story: You may never move abroad, but having the option changes how you negotiate and plan.
analogy.breaks: Avoiding all managed services sacrifices velocity, so be selective about where you pay for portability.

check.q: Why does a credible exit strategy matter even if you never leave?
